catalog_quote: In S[kwxwu7]mesh the first syllable of a morphologically simplex word is stressed if it contains a full vowel. ... schwa tends to resist being stressed in S[kwxwu7]mesh. When the initial vowel in a bisyllabic word is a schwa and the final vowel is something other than schwa, stress falls on the final non-schwa vowel. ... In a bisyllabic word with only schwas, stress falls on the leftmost schwa. ... The following tri-syllabic roots indicate that Skwxwu7mesh builds trochaic feet interatively since secondary stress falls on the final syllable and primary stress falls on the initial syllable. ... The basic stress rule is stress the leftmost full (i.e., non-schwa) vowel or schwa if there are no full vowels and alternating vowels thereafter. In other words, Skwxwu7mesh builds trochaic feet from left to right. The basic pattern is not always observed in Skwxwu7mesh. Weak suffixes follow the ba…
sweep_summary: Two title-hit items, both already listed. (1) Dyck 2004 (UVic PhD, 430 pp.) was already on file and was read in full at the key passages: default stress is penultimate and weight-conditioned (full vowel or schwa+resonant in the penult; else final), against Bar-el & Watt's leftmost-full-vowel analysis; this refines the catalog's kind=weight coding (weight upheld, edge orientation should be penult/right-bounded rather than initial) and is the best first-hand statement read; it supersedes Watt et al. 2000 as deciding source. (2) Demers & Horn 1978 IJAL 44(3):180-191 is paywalled (UChicago 403; Crossref metadata saved; Harvard HOLLIS access noted); its 1974 ICSNL typescript precursor on file states a quantity-insensitive penultimate rule ('Stress is generally penultimate in noncomplex, polysyllabic words', rule (3)), which contradicts the catalog's weight/leftmost-full-vowel statement and is the origin of the WALS/StressTyp 'penultimate' coding; medium priority to obtain the 1978 version. only direct fetches were possible.

new_statements.quote: stress is strongly motivated to fall on the penultimate syllables of Squamish words. [...] In propounding a default penultimate stress pattern for Squamish I side with the researchers who first worked on Squamish stress, namely Demers and Horn (1978) and Davis (1984a, 1984b) [...] I go against the more recent analysis of Bar-el and Watt (1998 [...]), who take the view that primary stress in Squamish falls on the leftmost full vowel of the prosodic word. [...] the evidence from the Squamish data in Kuipers (1967, 1969) favours a default penultimate stress theory. [...] stress in the phonological root surfaces on a penultimate syllable that contains either a full vowel or schwa followed by a resonant consonant.
new_statements.citation: Dyck, Ruth Anne (2004). Prosodic and Morphological Factors in Squamish (Skwxwu7mesh) Stress Assignment. PhD dissertation, University of Victoria (supervisor E. Czaykowska-Higgins; external examiner P. A. Shaw), 430 pp.
new_statements.locator: ch. 3 §3.0, pp. 74-75 (PDF pp. 86-87); same claim in Abstract p. ii and §3.1 p. 78 ('stress in Squamish is by default penultimate')
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, right-edge-oriented default: primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a root when that syllable is heavy (full vowel, or schwa + plain resonant); when the penult is a light schwa syllable (schwa before an obstruent or glottalized resonant) stress falls on the final syllable. Trisyllabic roots are mostly penult-stressed (55%, 82% when the penult has a full vowel); the initial-stress trisyllables cited by Watt (2000) are morphologically complex, not roots. Lexical accent on roots and suffixes overrides the phonological default in polymorphemic words. The catalog's kind=weight is upheld, but its 'first syllable... if it contains a full vowel' (left-edge) statement from Watt et al. 2000 holds only for disyllables and should be read as penult/right-edge bounded with a schwa+resonant heavy class.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Kind = weight is upheld and sharpened. Dyck 2004 (ch. 3-4, on the Kuipers 1967/1969 corpus) makes the conditioning explicit as syllable weight, not vowel quality per se: "The crucial factor, then, is not vowel predictability, but weight" (p. 78, PDF 90); constraint WSP1 "If weight, then stressed" (p. 91, PDF 103); plain resonants are weight-bearing, obstruents and glottalized resonants are not (p. 90, PDF 102). Root default: stress the penultimate syllable if it has weight (full vowel, or schwa + plain resonant); a weightless schwa penult (schwa + obstruent or glottalized resonant) is skipped…

audit.recode_to: Keep kind=weight (not fixed; StressTyp2 'penultimate, no secondary' stays contradicted) and wcls full-vs-reduced-vowel, but revise the sub-coding after reading Dyck 2004 ch. 3-4: edge 'unbounded/leftmost full vowel' -> right-edge bounded default (binary syllabic trochee aligned to the right edge: penult stressed if it has weight = full vowel or schwa+plain resonant, otherwise the final weighted syllable; leftmost schwa only in weightless words); 'heavy' should add schwa+resonant as heavy and note glottalized resonants pattern with obstruents; drop 'trisyllabic roots: initial primary' from prule (Dyck: majority of AAA trisyllabic roots are penultimate, e.g. q9uláyus, manác'i; Watt et al.'s málalòs is likely complex); keep the strong/accented-suffix override and add a caution that the left-oriented (Bar-el & Watt 1998, Watt et al. 2000) and penultimate (Demers & Horn 1978, Davis 1984, Dyck 2004) analyses coincide on disyllables and diverge only on the sparse 3+-syllable simplex forms.

sources.note: Full OT account of the whole stress system from Kuipers' (1967, 1969) data. Default stress in roots is PENULTIMATE and weight-conditioned: the penult is stressed when it contains a full vowel or a schwa followed by a (plain) resonant; otherwise stress goes to the final syllable (schwa before an obstruent or glottalized resonant in the penult). Abstract p. ii: roots 'tend to stress penultimate syllables whenever they contain either a full vowel or a schwa followed by a resonant consonant'. sources.quote: 'in bisyllabic roots, primary stress falls on the leftmost full vowel'; 'In roots that contain two schwas, the leftmost schwa will bear primary stress'; schwa-initial + full-vowel roots stress the second vowel; 'the data makes it clear that Skwxwú7mesh prefers to build trochaic feet. Since there is no evidence for weight sensitivity ... we will assume that coda consonants are non-moraic'; 'Inherently accented lexical suffixes receive primary stress without exception'; borrowed words keep source stress. This is the analysis Watt et al. 2000 summarize; same authors, same generalizations.

sources.citation: Demers, Richard A. & George M. Horn (1974). Stress in Squamish. Papers for the 9th ICSNL, pp. 196-209 (typescript precursor of Demers & Horn 1978, IJAL 44:180-191; data from Kuipers 1967).
sources.quote: p. 3: 'Stress is generally penultimate in noncomplex, polysyllabic words. ... (3) Basic Stress Assignment: V -> [+stress] / __ (C0V)C0 # ... Stress is not always penultimate, however', followed by stress-protraction over CC clusters, vowel harmony and cyclic application to morphological bracketing. This is the origin of StressTyp2/WALS 'penultimate'; it agrees with our coding only for full-vowel disyllables and says nothing quality-based in the basic rule (schwa effects handled derivationally).

sources.quote: [Demers & Horn 1974:3, vol. p. 198] Stress is generally penultimate in noncomplex, polysyllabic words. The following rule will account for the stress placement in all of the forms in (2): (3) Basic Stress Assignment: V ---> [+stress] / ___ (C0V)C0 # [...] The first expansion of the rule includes the material in the parentheses and will assign stress to the penultimate syllable. If the word is monosyllabic, this single syllable will also be stressed by the remaining part of the rule [...] Stress is not always penultimate, however.
